strengths: Principled problem formulation: Formalizing group-level training data attribution directly around the Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) counterfactual estimand and using machine unlearning as an efficient surrogate provides a conceptually clear and well-motivated framework.

Rigorous ground-truth evaluation: The authors conduct extensive comparisons against actual LOGO retrained models (on CIFAR-10 from scratch and on SD 1.5 via exposure-matched fine-tuning), providing a dependable gold standard that is often missing in training data attribution literature.

Thoughtful adaptation to conditional models: The paper correctly identifies why unconditional unlearning techniques (like ReTrack) cannot be naively transferred to conditional text-to-image settings due to prompt support shifts, and develops a sensible anchor redirection mechanism that preserves content while swapping style descriptors.

Empirical superiority over baselines: GUDA demonstrates consistent gains over aggregated gradient-based instance attribution methods (DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK), instance-level unlearning (Wang et al., 2024), and semantic similarity (CLIPA), especially on head-focused metrics like Top-1 and NDCG@3.

Comprehensive ablations and cost analysis: The appendix includes thorough sensitivity analysis across hyperparameters (epochs, forget loss weight, k-NN truncation, learning rate) and detailed wall-clock runtime breakdowns.
weaknesses: Scalability bottlenecks with respect to group count: While GUDA achieves substantial speedups over retraining from scratch, it still requires fine-tuning and storing N distinct unlearned diffusion models (one per group). When scaling to hundreds or thousands of concepts/artists, maintaining and evaluating N separate models (with N ELBO computations per query) remains computationally and storage-wise demanding.

Pretraining leakage in the large-scale benchmark: On the UnlearnCanvas / SD 1.5 benchmark, the full and LOGO models are fine-tuned from the public SD 1.5 checkpoint. Because SD 1.5 was pretrained on massive web-scale data (LAION) that likely already contains representations of many of these artistic styles, the LOGO counterfactual does not isolate the complete removal of the style concept from the foundational representations.

Moderate ranking correlation with gold standard: Although GUDA outperforms baselines, the absolute ranking alignment remains modest (Top-1 agreement is 45.6% on UnlearnCanvas; Spearman rank correlation is ~0.24 on UnlearnCanvas and ~0.27 on CIFAR-10), indicating that fine-tuning unlearning proxies still exhibit non-trivial divergence from true counterfactual retraining.

Restriction to disjoint, static partitions: The methodology assumes data is cleanly partitioned into disjoint semantic groups {D_k}. In real-world data attribution scenarios, examples frequently belong to multiple overlapping categories (e.g., shared artists, genres, subject matters, or eras), and groups may need to be queried dynamically rather than pre-partitioned prior to unlearning.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: The paper clearly articulates why group-wise counterfactual attribution is distinct from aggregating instance-level attribution (due to representation sharing and non-linear collective effects), providing a sound conceptual framing.

Principled bridge between counterfactual modeling and unlearning: Using machine unlearning as a fast surrogate for Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) retraining is conceptually elegant and pragmatically effective.

Thoughtful adaptation to conditional generation: Recognizing that unconditional unlearning (like ReTrack) cannot directly apply to conditional text-to-image models due to prompt distribution shift, the authors design an effective anchor redirection mechanism (GUDA-C) that preserves content while substituting style descriptors.

Solid empirical validation against gold-standard oracles: Evaluating against actual LOGO models on CIFAR-10 and exposure-matched fine-tuned LOGO models on Stable Diffusion 1.5 provides concrete evidence that GUDA accurately approximates counterfactual influence, substantially outperforming CLIP similarity and instance-level baselines (DAS, D-TRAK, Wang et al.).
Substantial computational speedups: GUDA achieves a ~100x speedup over LOGO retraining on CIFAR-10 and offers decoupled, amortized preprocessing that makes query-time attribution fast and scalable.
weaknesses: Scalability with the number of groups ($N$): While unlearning is much faster than retraining from scratch, GUDA still scales linearly in both unlearning runs and model storage with $N$ (requiring $N$ separate checkpoints and $N$ model forward passes per query). Discussion or exploration of parameter-efficient adaptation (e.g., LoRA-based unlearning) to reduce storage and training overhead when scaling to hundreds of groups would be valuable.

Disjoint partition assumption: The framework currently assumes training data is partitioned into mutually exclusive groups ($\mathcal{D} =  igcup_k \mathcal{D}_k$). In real-world multimodal datasets, images often possess overlapping group attributes (e.g., overlapping styles, concepts, and subjects).

Overall ranking correlation remains relatively low: While GUDA performs well on head-focused metrics (Top-1, NDCG@3), the Spearman rank correlation across all groups remains around 0.24–0.27 on both CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas, indicating that tail ranking remains noisy across all evaluated methods.

Evaluation scope on Stable Diffusion: Due to the high cost of LOGO retraining, the evaluation is limited to 16 styles and 320 queries on synthetic prompt templates, leaving questions about how the unlearning proxy behaves under highly diverse, in-the-wild web-scale text-image distributions.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: The paper clearly formalizes group-wise training data attribution for diffusion models around a Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) counterfactual estimand, correctly pointing out the non-additivity and scalability failure modes of aggregating instance-level influences.

Methodological innovation: Connecting counterfactual data attribution to machine unlearning provides an elegant computational bridge. Furthermore, addressing the failure of unconditional unlearning (ReTrack) in conditional text-to-image diffusion via weighted style-selection anchors (AWSS) is conceptually sound and well-reasoned.

Rigorous gold-standard validation: The authors directly train actual LOGO models (both from scratch on CIFAR-10 and fine-tuned on Stable Diffusion 1.5) to serve as gold-standard oracles, enabling direct and convincing fidelity benchmarking.

Solid empirical results and thorough ablations: GUDA consistently outperforms semantic similarity (CLIPA) and gradient/unlearning-based baselines (D-TRAK, DAS, Wang et al.) on head-focused attribution metrics, supported by comprehensive ablation studies on unlearning epochs, regularization, and aggregation methods.
weaknesses: Linear scaling in the number of groups: Although GUDA is substantially faster than retraining from scratch (achieving ~100x speedup on CIFAR-10), it still requires fine-tuning and storing N distinct unlearned models for N groups. For large-scale deployment with hundreds or thousands of groups, checkpoint storage and linear ELBO evaluation cost remain significant practical hurdles.

Pre-training contamination in text-to-image evaluation: In the UnlearnCanvas experiments, the base model is Stable Diffusion 1.5, which already contains broad knowledge of artistic styles from web-scale pre-training. While the authors evaluate LOGO via fine-tuning proxy, pre-existing stylistic representations could partially confound the counterfactual style attribution.

Assumption of disjoint groups: The formulation assumes a clean partition of the training dataset into disjoint groups {D_k}. In real-world data attribution settings, concepts, styles, and data ownership often have significant overlaps.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper clearly defines group-wise counterfactual attribution for diffusion models around a Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) estimand, addressing key shortcomings of instance-level score aggregation (such as nonlinearity and poor scalability).

Principled and practical framework: Framing machine unlearning as a fast surrogate for LOGO counterfactual models is conceptually sound. Connecting ReTrack's redirection to importance sampling of the retain distribution provides a solid theoretical motivation for the unconditional setting.

Effective conditional design: The paper identifies the prompt distribution mismatch in conditional generation when a style/group is omitted, and introduces an effective anchor redirection mechanism (AWSS) that fixes content while re-anchoring styles based on CLIP similarity.

Rigorous evaluation against gold-standard oracles: The authors explicitly train actual LOGO counterfactual models on CIFAR-10 and Stable Diffusion fine-tunes to establish ground truth, enabling direct fidelity evaluation (Top-k, NDCG@3, MRR) rather than relying solely on proxy correlation.

Comprehensive validation and ablations: The appendix provides extensive and well-executed analyses, including comparisons between the ELBO surrogate and probability-flow ODE likelihoods, anchor design ablations, sensitivity to unlearning parameters, wall-clock timing breakdowns, and robustness to noisy group partitions.
weaknesses: Linear scaling with the number of groups: While GUDA is significantly faster than retraining from scratch (~100x on CIFAR-10, ~5.2x on SD 1.5 fine-tuning), constructing counterfactual models still scales as O(N) unlearning runs. For thousands of granular groups/artists, maintaining and storing N separate model checkpoints remains computationally demanding.

Assumption of disjoint group partitions: The framework assumes training data is partitioned into distinct groups. In real-world web-scale text-to-image datasets, concepts, artistic influences, and styles overlap substantially and lack clean boundaries.

Moderate absolute fidelity on complex text-to-image models: On UnlearnCanvas with Stable Diffusion 1.5, GUDA achieves 45.6% Top-1 agreement with the LOGO oracle. While this comfortably beats baselines (e.g., CLIPA at 33.8%), it highlights remaining gaps between unlearning approximations and true counterfactual retraining in high-dimensional multimodal spaces.

strengths: Principled and clear formulation: The paper formalizes group-wise training data attribution for diffusion models around a clear Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) counterfactual estimand, elegantly reframing machine unlearning as an efficient computational proxy for model-level counterfactual estimation rather than solely as a concept deletion tool.

Methodological soundness across settings: The paper tackles both unconditional and conditional diffusion settings carefully. In particular, it correctly identifies the prompt-distribution shift inherent to conditional group removal and proposes an effective weighted style-selection anchor redirection (AWSS) mechanism.

Rigorous evaluation against actual LOGO oracles: Unlike many attribution papers that rely solely on heuristic proxies or synthetic unit tests, this work goes through the compute-intensive effort of retraining full LOGO models (from scratch on CIFAR-10 and fine-tuned on UnlearnCanvas with Stable Diffusion 1.5) to serve as gold-standard ground truth.

Comprehensive validation and ablations: The appendix provides extensive and well-designed analyses, including comparing the ELBO proxy against an aligned Probability-Flow ODE log-likelihood oracle (Table 13), evaluating robustness against noisy group partitions (Table 16), and ablating anchor redirection strategies, unlearning epochs, learning rates, and aggregation functions.

Strong head-metric results and efficiency: GUDA substantially outperforms semantic similarity (CLIPA) and gradient-/instance-based attribution methods on key head-identification metrics (Top-1, MRR, NDCG@3) while delivering orders-of-magnitude wall-clock speedups over LOGO retraining.
weaknesses: Linear scaling with the number of groups ($N$): Although unlearning is significantly faster than retraining from scratch or long fine-tuning, GUDA still requires running $N$ independent unlearning fine-tuning runs and storing $N$ checkpoint models. When the number of groups grows into the hundreds or thousands, this amortized preprocessing cost and storage requirement remains non-trivial without parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA).

Moderate absolute accuracy on conditional text-to-image: On UnlearnCanvas (Stable Diffusion 1.5), GUDA achieves 45.6% Top-1 agreement against the LOGO oracle. While this comfortably beats CLIPA (33.8%) and Wang et al. (4.7%), it indicates that unlearning remains an imperfect surrogate for full retraining in high-dimensional text-conditioned settings.

Scope of group definitions: The experimental validation is restricted to disjoint, pre-defined groups (CIFAR-10 classes and distinct artistic styles in UnlearnCanvas). In practical open-web datasets, groups are frequently overlapping, multi-attribute, or hierarchical, which is acknowledged as a limitation but remains unaddressed in the methodology.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated formulation: The paper formalizes group-wise training data attribution through a Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) counterfactual estimand using ELBO differences, providing a clear conceptual foundation that addresses the non-additivity and non-scalability of aggregating instance-level attribution methods.

Rigorous ground-truth evaluation: Unlike many attribution papers that rely solely on heuristic proxies or synthetic corruptions, the authors explicitly retrain actual Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) oracle diffusion models on both CIFAR-10 and Stable Diffusion 1.5 (fine-tuning proxy), providing an empirical gold standard to benchmark against.

Thoughtful adaptation to conditional text-to-image models: The AWSS (Anchor-based Weighted Style-Selection) module addresses the condition-distribution mismatch inherent when extending redirection-based unlearning to text-conditional settings where prompt distributions shift.

Extensive empirical analysis and thorough appendix: The paper provides comprehensive ablation studies (hyperparameters, aggregation baselines, noisy partitions) and directly validates the ELBO surrogate against a probability-flow ODE log-likelihood oracle in Appendix D.5, showing strong correlation and ranking consistency.

Substantial speedup: GUDA demonstrates a ~100x speedup over retraining from scratch on CIFAR-10 and a >5x speedup over fine-tuning LOGO on Stable Diffusion, while outperforming gradient-based and instance-level baselines on head-focused attribution metrics.
weaknesses: Storage and scaling bottleneck with group count: Although GUDA is substantially faster than full LOGO retraining, it still scales linearly with the number of groups $N$, requiring fine-tuning and storing $N$ distinct diffusion models. For datasets containing hundreds or thousands of concepts/styles, storing and managing separate model checkpoints remains a significant practical burden.

Limited algorithmic novelty in unlearning operators: The core unlearning engine for the unconditional setting is directly adopted from ReTrack (Shi et al., 2026), and the conditional method adapts this via CLIP-based text substitution. As acknowledged by the authors, the technical contribution centers on the attribution framework and estimand rather than a fundamentally new unlearning mechanism.

Evaluation scale is constrained to modest group counts: Empirical results are shown on 10 classes for CIFAR-10 and 16 evaluated styles for UnlearnCanvas. Validating on settings with larger candidate groups or fine-grained/overlapping boundaries remains an important open challenge.

Artificial nature of unconditional class attribution: Evaluating group attribution on unconditional CIFAR-10 (where the model is trained unconditionally across classes) is primarily a synthetic proof-of-concept; in unconditional settings, practitioners rarely query 'which class influenced this unconditional sample' in the same way as prompt-driven generation.
